opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a big question, and I'll give you my honest view, with the caveat that anyone who predicts ten years out in robotics with too much confidence is probably wrong.

I think the next decade will play out in roughly three phases.

In the first few years, the main change will happen in the research labs and in the "brains" of robots more than in our homes. Over the last couple of years we've seen large models, the same kind of foundation models behind chatbots, start to work for robot control. Vision-language-action models can take a camera image and an instruction like "put the apple in the bowl" and produce motor commands. They're still clumsy and unreliable, but they generalize in ways that classical robotics never did. Robots used to be programmed task by task. Now we can start to imagine one model that knows a little about a lot of tasks. I think the next two or three years will focus on making that reliability go from, say, sixty or seventy percent success up to ninety-nine-plus percent. That last stretch is the hardest part, just like with self-driving cars.

The biggest bottleneck there is data. Language models had the whole internet. Robotics has no internet of physical interaction. So a lot of the progress will come from creative ways to get data: simulation, which is an area I've worked in a lot, teleoperation at scale, learning from human videos, and robots that are already deployed collecting experience. Whoever builds the best data flywheel will probably lead.

In the middle of the decade, I expect general-purpose robots to show up first in semi-structured commercial settings rather than homes: warehouses, logistics, factories, maybe retail back rooms and hospitals. These places have real labor shortages and clear economics, the environment is somewhat controlled, and there's someone to supervise and maintain the robot. Mistakes are tolerable there. A dropped box is fine; a robot that knocks over a toddler is not.

The home is the hardest environment, and I think it comes last. Every home is different, cluttered, full of fragile things, pets, and kids. Safety and cost both matter enormously. A family won't pay the price of a car for a robot that folds laundry slowly and sometimes fails. So by the end of the decade, I'd guess we'll see early-adopter home robots, probably in narrower roles at first: tidying, fetching, maybe helping elderly people live independently. That last use case could be really meaningful, especially in aging societies like China, Japan, and much of Europe.

On form factor, people get very excited about humanoids. There's a real argument for them: our world is built for human bodies, and human video data maps more naturally onto a humanoid. But I don't think the humanoid shape is required. Wheeled bases with one or two good arms might be more practical and cheaper for a lot of tasks for quite a while. The intelligence matters more than the body.

One more thing I'd emphasize is hardware. People sometimes assume AI will solve everything, but good hands, durable actuators, safe motors, and low cost are still very hard engineering problems. Dexterous manipulation in particular is still far from human level. Software is moving fast right now; hardware has to catch up and become cheap through scale, similar to what happened with electric vehicles.

So my summary: in ten years I don't think every home will have a Rosie the robot. But I do think general-purpose robots will be a normal sight in workplaces, the technology will have crossed a real threshold of usefulness, and homes will be at the start of the adoption curve, much like smartphones around 2008. That's what makes this an exciting time to work in the field.

r001.rationale: The response expects the next two or three years to focus on improving reliability, but does not predict a broadly recognized “GPT moment” for general-purpose robots.

r002.rationale: It predicts robots will appear first in semi-structured commercial settings such as warehouses and factories, with home use coming later.

r003.rationale: It contrasts task-by-task programming with models that can handle a range of tasks and generalize beyond fixed actions.

r004.rationale: It forecasts only early-adopter home robots in narrower roles by the end of the decade and says homes will be at the start of adoption, not that robots will enter homes widely.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Let me start with a caveat: anyone who gives you a confident ten-year timeline for robotics is probably wrong, including me. So let me talk about trajectories rather than dates.

I think the first thing to understand is why this moment feels different from the robotics hype cycles we've been through before. For decades, the bottleneck was never the hardware. You could build a very capable arm or even a legged robot twenty years ago. The bottleneck was the brain. Every new task meant a team of engineers writing controllers by hand, tuning them for months, and the result would break the moment the environment changed slightly. That's why robots lived in factories behind cages, where the world could be made predictable.

What changed is that we now have a recipe for learning general behavior from data. We saw it in language, we saw it in vision, and the question for our field became: can we do the same thing for physical action? The early evidence says yes. If you train a single model across many robots, many tasks, many environments, it starts to generalize in ways that no hand-written controller ever did. It can pick up an object it has never seen, in a kitchen it has never been in. That's still fragile today, but the slope matters more than the current point on the curve.

Now, what does that mean for the next decade? I'd break it into three phases, and they'll overlap.

The first phase, which we're already in, is structured environments with a lot of repetition. Warehouses, logistics, manufacturing, some parts of agriculture. These are places where the economics are clear, the tasks are somewhat bounded, and a robot that works ninety-five percent of the time with a human handling exceptions is already valuable. This is where learning-based robots will prove themselves commercially first, because the tolerance for failure is manageable.

The second phase is semi-structured spaces that humans share: hospitals, hotels, restaurants, elder care facilities, retail backrooms. Here the environment is messier, people are moving around, and the tasks are more varied. But there's still institutional ownership, meaning someone is responsible for maintenance, safety, and deployment. I expect we'll see real deployments here in the second half of the decade, probably starting with narrower tasks like delivery, restocking, and cleaning, and gradually expanding.

The third phase is the home, and honestly, that's the hardest one. People always ask when they'll get a robot that does their dishes and folds their laundry. The home is the most unstructured environment there is. Every home is different, things are constantly moving, there are children and pets, and the tolerance for error is extremely low. If a robot knocks over a glass in a warehouse, that's a cost. If it knocks over a glass in your kitchen near your kid, that's a trust problem, and trust is very hard to rebuild. I think useful home robots are plausible within ten years, but they'll start simple and narrow, and they'll earn their way into more tasks slowly.

There are a few things I think will determine how fast all of this happens.

Data is the big one. Language models had the internet. Robots don't have an internet of physical experience. So the field is attacking this from several directions at once: simulation, where you can generate enormous amounts of experience cheaply; teleoperation, where humans demonstrate tasks; video of humans doing things, which is abundant but hard to translate into robot action; and eventually robots collecting their own data in the real world. I think the winning approach will combine all of these, and the flywheel starts turning once there are enough robots deployed to learn from their own mistakes.

Hardware is the second. Hardware has to become cheaper, safer, and more reliable, and that happens with scale. Cost curves in robotics look a lot like other hardware industries: once volume goes up, cost comes down dramatically. But you need a reason to produce at volume first, which brings us back to finding those early applications that work.

The third is safety and the interface with humans. A robot that is physically capable but that people don't understand or feel comfortable around won't be adopted. So a lot of the work isn't just about making robots more capable. It's about making them predictable, making their intentions legible, letting them explain what they're about to do, and letting people correct them in natural ways, through speech or a quick gesture. The convergence with language models actually helps enormously here, because now the robot can understand an instruction like "be careful, the floor is wet" and change its behavior.

One more thing I'd push back on gently is the obsession with the humanoid form factor. Humanoids make sense as a general-purpose platform in a world built for humans, and I think they'll be part of the picture. But a lot of the value in the next decade will come from robots that don't look like people at all: mobile manipulators on wheels, specialized arms, quadrupeds for inspection. The form should follow the task, and the intelligence layer can be shared across all of them. That's actually one of the most exciting implications of foundation models for robotics: the same brain can drive many bodies.

So if I had to summarize: over the next ten years I expect robots to go from novelty to infrastructure in industrial and commercial settings, to become genuinely helpful in shared public spaces, and to make their first real, if modest, entry into homes. The progress won't be linear. There will be moments where it looks like it's stalling and moments where it leaps. But the fundamental ingredients are finally in place, and that's what makes me optimistic in a way I wouldn't have been even five years ago.

r001.rationale: It describes current progress in learning-based robotics but gives no prediction of a broadly recognized “GPT moment” within two or three years.

r002.rationale: It predicts deployments will prove themselves first in industrial and commercial settings, with home robots arriving later.

r003.rationale: It contrasts learning-based robots that generalize across tasks and environments with hand-written controllers that break when conditions change.

r004.rationale: It predicts useful home robots may appear within ten years, but describes their entry as modest and gradual, not widespread.

astra-6.text:
I think over the next decade, we’ll see robots become useful in a growing range of tasks, but progress will be uneven. A robot might learn a new skill quickly, yet making that skill reliable in a messy, unfamiliar environment is much harder. That gap between an impressive demonstration and something you can depend on every day is really important.

I expect adoption to happen first in more structured environments, like warehouses and factories, where the tasks are clear and you can measure the value. As the technology improves, robots can gradually take on more varied work. Homes are especially challenging because every home is different, and robots have to operate safely around people, pets, and fragile objects.

The exciting possibility is that we won’t need to program every behavior separately. Robots could learn from demonstrations and experience, then use what they’ve learned to handle new tasks. But that still requires progress in both intelligence and hardware: dexterity, reliability, cost, and safety all matter.

So I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t assume that everyone will have a robot doing all their housework in ten years. I’d expect more robots that do a useful set of tasks well, with those capabilities expanding over time. Their entry into everyday life may feel gradual—first you encounter one at work or in a service setting, and eventually having one help at home becomes practical.

r001.rationale: It predicts gradual progress over the next decade, but gives no two- or three-year “GPT moment” when people broadly recognize robots are arriving.

r002.rationale: It expects adoption first in structured settings such as warehouses and factories, with home use becoming practical later.

r003.rationale: It says robots could learn from demonstrations and experience and use that learning to handle new tasks, distinguishing them from systems limited to one predetermined task.

r004.rationale: It does not predict wide home entry within roughly ten years; it says household adoption may come eventually and cautions against expecting everyone to have a housework robot in that timeframe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think over the next decade, we’ll see robots become useful in increasingly varied settings, but it will happen gradually. A robot that can do a demonstration in the lab is very different from a robot that can work reliably every day around people.

My expectation is that adoption will start in more structured environments—factories, warehouses, perhaps some commercial settings—where the tasks are clear and the value is measurable. Homes are much harder. Every home is different, objects move around, and people have very different expectations. Even something like putting away laundry requires a surprising amount of perception, dexterity, and judgment.

The exciting opportunity is that robots could learn many skills using a shared foundation, instead of us engineering each task separately. Simulation and experience in the real world can help, but reliability, safety, and cost still have to improve together.

So I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t expect every household to have a robot that can do everything in ten years. I would expect more people to encounter robots doing useful work, and some to have robots at home that handle a limited set of chores well. That would already be a meaningful step toward general-purpose robots.

r001.rationale: The response gives no prediction of a broadly recognized robotics breakthrough within two or three years.

r002.rationale: It says adoption will start in factories, warehouses, and some commercial settings, while homes are harder.

r003.rationale: It describes robots learning many skills from a shared foundation instead of engineering each task separately, conveying capacity beyond fixed, task-specific automation.

r004.rationale: It expects only some homes to have robots handling limited chores within ten years and explicitly does not expect every household to have one; it does not predict wide home entry on that horizon.
